findings.lesson_text: When the Inspector suggests that 'these girls aren't cheap labour — they're people,' Birling dismisses the comment entirely. This exchange encapsulates the play's central conflict: Birling sees workers as a cost to be minimised; the Inspector sees them as human beings with rights.
findings.issue: The line 'these girls aren't cheap labour — they're people' is attributed to the Inspector, but it is Sheila Birling's line, spoken in Act 1. A student memorising this from the lesson would cite the wrong speaker in their exam.
findings.canonical_truth: The line is spoken by Sheila Birling in Act 1, not by Inspector Goole. It is one of the most-cited Sheila quotations on every GCSE revision platform and is confirmed as Sheila's across all authoritative sources.

findings.lesson_text: Key Fact: The Inspector's line 'these girls aren't cheap labour — they're people' directly challenges Birling's capitalist worldview. It is the first statement of the play's central argument: that human beings have inherent value and cannot be treated as disposable resources. Birling's inability to understand this point is precisely what Priestley wants the audience to reject.
findings.issue: The Key Fact box repeats the misattribution: 'the Inspector's line' for a quote that belongs to Sheila. The lesson attributes this quote to the Inspector twice — once in the narrative and once in the Key Fact box.
findings.canonical_truth: Sheila Birling says this line in Act 1. Inspector Goole does not say it. Misattributing it to the Inspector in both the text and the Key Fact box compounds the error.

findings.lesson_text: The Inspector's rebuke is quiet but devastating: 'these girls aren't cheap labour — they're people.'
findings.issue: The line 'these girls aren't cheap labour — they're people' is attributed to the Inspector, but it is Sheila Birling's line. This is the same error as OCR L02, appearing in a separate board's lesson.
findings.canonical_truth: Sheila says this line in Act 1 as part of her moral awakening. It is not spoken by the Inspector. Attributing it to the Inspector in the Eduqas lesson also risks students writing incorrect speaker attributions in their Eduqas exam.

findings.lesson_title: Act 2: Gerald and Mrs Birling Exposed
findings.lesson_text: Gerald eventually confesses. He met Daisy at the Palace Bar... Eva 'was very grateful' and 'gave me a look that was nothing less than adoring.'
findings.issue: The phrase 'gave me a look that was nothing less than adoring' is presented as a direct quotation from Gerald (in quotation marks) but does not appear in the play. Gerald's actual words about Eva are 'She was young and pretty and warm-hearted – and intensely grateful' and 'I became at once the most important person in her life'. The fabricated quote does not appear in any authoritative resource for the play.
findings.canonical_truth: Gerald's actual quotes about Eva/Daisy in Act 2: 'She was young and pretty and warm-hearted – and intensely grateful' and 'I became at once the most important person in her life' and 'I didn't feel about her as she felt about me.' The 'adoring look' phrase is not in the play.

findings.lesson_title: Act 3: The Ending and the Phone Call
findings.lesson_text: Mr Birling, Mrs Birling and Gerald immediately begin trying to prove the Inspector was a fraud. They telephone the Chief Constable, who confirms there is no Inspector Goole on the force.
findings.issue: The lesson says 'they telephone the Chief Constable' to confirm there is no Inspector Goole. In the play, it is Gerald who goes out and makes enquiries, and he speaks to a police sergeant (not the Chief Constable directly) to establish the Inspector's non-existence. Birling does have a connection to the Chief Constable, but the lesson compresses the sequence in a way that implies the discovery comes from telephoning the Chief Constable, which oversimplifies the scene.
findings.canonical_truth: Gerald leaves the house to make enquiries and discovers there is no Inspector Goole on the local police force. The family also rings the Infirmary to confirm no girl has died. The 'telephone the Chief Constable' phrasing is a compression that may mislead students about who acts and how.

findings.lesson_text: When Gerald ended the affair, he gave her money and 'left her — turning her out.'
findings.issue: The phrase 'left her — turning her out' is presented in quotation marks as if a direct quotation from the play, but this specific phrasing is not confirmed in the play text. Gerald ends the affair and gives Eva money, but 'turning her out' implies eviction rather than a relationship ending. No authoritative source confirms this as a direct quote.
findings.canonical_truth: Gerald ends the affair when he has to go away for several weeks on business and gives Eva money to keep her going. The play does not use the phrase 'turning her out' in Gerald's account. Eva accepts the end of the relationship without blaming Gerald.

findings.lesson_text: Mrs Birling insists that the real responsibility lies with 'the father of the child' and that he should be made an example of, publicly shamed, and forced to 'confess in public his responsibility.'
findings.issue: The phrase 'confess in public his responsibility' is presented as a direct quotation in quotation marks, but it is not confirmed as Mrs Birling's exact words in the play. Her known lines are that the father should be 'made an example of' and 'dealt with very severely.' The specific 'confess in public' phrase is not substantiated.
findings.canonical_truth: Mrs Birling says the father should be 'made an example of' and 'dealt with very severely.' The phrase 'confess in public his responsibility' appears to be a paraphrase or invention presented as a direct quote.

findings.lesson_text: An Inspector Calls premiered at the Kamerny Theatre in Moscow on 1 October 1945, before its London debut at the New Theatre on 1 October 1946.
findings.issue: The lesson gives exact dates ('1 October 1945' and '1 October 1946') for both premiere dates. Wikipedia confirms the Moscow and London premieres in 1945 and 1946 respectively, but the specific date '1 October' for both venues cannot be independently verified and may be incorrect. The coincidence of the same date for both premieres is suspicious.
findings.canonical_truth: An Inspector Calls did premiere in Moscow (Kamerny Theatre) in 1945 before London's New Theatre in 1946. The exact premiere dates within those years cannot be confirmed from the sources checked. The claim that both opened on '1 October' may be inaccurate — this cannot be verified with confidence.

findings.lesson_text: John Boynton Priestley was born in Bradford in 1894 into a middle-class family. He fought in the First World War and was badly injured.
findings.issue: The lesson says Priestley 'was badly injured' in WWI. Sources confirm Priestley was wounded and gassed during WWI, though some describe his injuries as serious rather than 'badly injured'. The broader issue is 'middle-class family' — Priestley's father was a schoolteacher (lower-middle class). Minor contextual imprecision.
findings.canonical_truth: Priestley was born in Bradford in 1894. His father was a schoolmaster. He was wounded in WWI. The description 'middle-class family' is a slight stretch — his background was lower-middle class or working-class professional. Low severity.

findings.lesson_title: Characters: Sheila, Eric, Gerald and Mrs Birling
findings.lesson_text: Priestley uses Gerald to show that aristocratic privilege is just as resistant to change as middle-class capitalism.
findings.issue: The lesson describes Gerald's background as 'aristocratic privilege'. In the play, the Croft family are described as 'an old country family — landed people' — landed gentry rather than aristocracy proper. Landed gentry and aristocracy are distinct social categories, though both are upper class. This is a minor imprecision.
findings.canonical_truth: Gerald's family (the Crofts) are landed gentry — 'an old country family — landed people' in Birling's description. They are upper-class but not technically aristocracy (no title is mentioned). 'Aristocratic' is an overstatement but a minor one.
